Program: Relay Wichita
City: Wichita
Contract (the brief): $500,000 (the brief: "The city is offering $500,000.")
Pilot: 90 days (the brief: "You are designing a 90-day Wichita pilot.")
Marketing reserve: $100,000 (the brief: "$100,000 is reserved for marketing, trust-building, and adoption.")
Beneficiary unit: people

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Wichita's system is fast once a person is matched. Housing takes 45 days on average, against 176 nationally 📊 community snapshot. People fall out between doors. Only 17 of 87 emergency beds are reachable 📊 system status, and 42% of former foster youth on the KanCare extension lose coverage 📊 transition programs. Relay Wichita spends $500K on four things: a transition-bottleneck dashboard, 2 staff who own each case until the next door confirms receipt, a landlord desk for NEXTenant partners, and a $100K trust-and-adoption reserve. It serves 120 people in Year 1 at $3,503 per person (estimate). Without the program, outcomes valued at an estimated $464.54K partial would not happen over 3 years.

CRISIS:
Wichita counted 736 people homeless on the 2025 Point-in-Time night. Of these, 195 were unsheltered, and the total was up 6.11% from 2024 📊 community snapshot. Volume is not the core failure. The local rate of 14 per 10,000 residents sits below the national 23 per 10,000 residents. Placements average 45 days, against 176 days nationally. The failure is at the handoffs: Only 17 of 87 emergency beds are reachable tonight 📊 system status. Only 38% of the 3,257 people served were housed within the year 📊 community snapshot. Youth leaving foster care hit a cliff. Homelessness reaches 42% by age 21. That is above the national official poverty rate of 11.1%, which is a different measure, shown for scale. Former foster youth on the KanCare extension lose coverage at 42%. That is above the national uninsured rate of 8%, also a different measure 📊 community snapshot, transition programs. Second Light, the intended front door, still places referrals by phone because HMIS bed-matching is not live 📊 shelter inventory, system status.
Maya, age 19 and newly out of foster care, can reach CrossRoads, the city's only round-the-clock youth shelter, with 10 of 12 beds in use. Her state ID needs a birth certificate, a Social Security card and proof of residency she cannot show, which takes at least 31 days of processing. Each office visit means a $50 monthly bus pass on 30-60-minute headways with no Sunday service 📊 stabilization docs. These barriers feed each other: income poverty makes the pass unaffordable, the missing ID blocks the bank account and job that would fix the income, and the transit gap turns each 2-4-hour DCF wait into a lost day of work. If she spoke Spanish, Second Light and CrossRoads intake (English only) could not serve her, which pushes her toward 211 Kansas, Open Door, DCF or Center of Hope and adds another handoff 📊 intake network. Every move also risks her KanCare extension, which 42% of enrollees lose through notices sent to old addresses; the data holds no neighborhood income or poverty rates, so none is cited for where she lives.

SOLUTION:
Relay Wichita builds no new beds. It makes the existing ones reachable and keeps people attached after each counter visit. It has four parts. Bottleneck dashboard. It reads the 381 beds and 210 program slots in the records and applies each site's own entry gates. It then shows which of the 55 free beds and 76 free slots a given person can actually use. This gives Second Light the matching layer its HMIS integration has not yet delivered 📊 shelter inventory, transition programs, system status. Case ownership. A navigator owns each case until the next door confirms receipt. The navigator runs a document track that starts with a City ID in 1 day. The navigator also runs a benefits-continuity checklist: SNAP's 7-day expedited processing, KanCare address updates, and DCF IL and ETV enrollment 📊 stabilization docs. Landlord desk. NEXTenant partners get one named contact and a response standard. The desk pairs rapid rehousing with Housing First at HumanKind Villas 📊 rehousing options. Trust and adoption reserve. The $100K reserve funds youth peer ambassadors, landlord trust-building and partner adoption. H.O.T., Open Door, 211 Kansas, DCF IL and City ID remain the doors. Relay supplies the warm handoff that today ends at each counter.
Of the 3,257 people the homelessness system served in FY 2023–24, 736 were homeless on the 2025 Point-in-Time night. The program targets 120 people in Year 1, scaling to 152 by Year 3. Former foster youth are prioritized from the 583 Kansas youth who age out each year 📊 community snapshot. The data is county-wide for Wichita–Sedgwick County and has no area-level breakdown, so no monitored-area count is used anywhere in this proposal.

COST OF INACTION:
Without the program, the outcomes it would produce do not happen. For each year, each valued outcome is counted among that year's people served (its rate × the people), times its value, less deadweight (25%). Year 1 (120 served): $135.96K partial. Year 2 (138 served): $156.36K partial. Year 3 (152 served): $172.22K partial. Cumulative over 3 years: $464.54K partial. Not in this figure — material, not valued: Exit to stable housing with a confirmed next placement (The data gives no local cost per shelter night, per eviction or per placement, so any proxy would be a figure the data does not support.).

KEY METRICS:
  People in Year 1: 120
  Cost per person: $3,503
  SROI ratio: 0.28 : 1 (below 1: less counted social value than cost, on the outcomes modeled)
    partial — material, not valued: Exit to stable housing with a confirmed next placement (The data gives no local cost per shelter night, per eviction or per placement, so any proxy would be a figure the data does not support.)

EVIDENCE FINDINGS:
  - Beds exist on paper, not at the door: Alert status-001 counts 17 of 87 emergency beds as reachable (19.5%). The facility records list 55 free beds of 381 online, but referral rules, breathalyzer screening and household restrictions remove most of them. Union Rescue Mission's intake gate filters out roughly a third of would-be intakes. This pattern mirrors the condition-of-entry exclusion documented in national Housing First research, where people turned away at a sobriety or referral gate are back outside within hours of asking for a bed. (source: 📊 system status, shelter inventory)
  - The age-out cliff for foster youth: Homelessness among youth from foster care rises from 17% by age 17 to 29% by age 19 and 42% by age 21. Kansas sees 583 youth age out each year. DCF IL benefits stop the day a youth turns 21, and close to 4 in 10 participants lose contact within 90 days post-exit. CrossRoads reports about 35% of exits without a confirmed placement because BRIDGES has only eight units. This pattern mirrors the age-out cliff documented nationally in foster-care transition research, where youth lose case management, stipends and housing support within 90 days of an exit tied to a birthday rather than to stability. (source: 📊 community snapshot, transition programs)
  - Coverage lost through the mailbox: 142 former foster youth are enrolled in the KanCare extension, which carries no income test. Even so, 42% drop out, overwhelmingly through recertification notices sent to old addresses. Re-enrollment requires an in-person DCF visit with a 2-4-hour wait on weekdays only 📊 transition programs, intake network. This pattern mirrors administrative churn documented nationally in Medicaid, where eligible people lose coverage at the next renewal after a move because the notice never reaches them. (source: 📊 transition programs, stabilization docs, intake network)
  - Documents gate everything downstream: From no documents, a Kansas state ID takes at least 31 days of processing. The steps are a birth certificate (14 days), a Social Security card (10 days) and the ID itself (7 days). All of this comes before the proof of residency that unsheltered applicants rarely hold. Without the ID, banking, leases and KanCare applications stall. This pattern mirrors the documentation trap documented nationally among people exiting homelessness, where a lost birth certificate stalls benefits, jobs and leases for weeks after displacement. (source: 📊 stabilization docs)

BRIEF — QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS (the competition's own items and this page's answers):
- Q: Transition bottleneck dashboard
  A: The dashboard reads the shelter, intake, program, document and rehousing records. For each person, it shows which of the 381 listed beds and 210 program slots they can actually enter once each site's gates are applied. Today it would show 55 free beds overall but only 17 of 87 emergency beds reachable. It would also flag BRIDGES at eight units with a six-week wait and HumanKind's 8-12-week waitlist as the permanent-housing choke point. It gives Second Light the matching layer its HMIS integration has not yet delivered, and it logs every handoff so the city can see where cases stall.
- Q: Use-of-funds model
  A: Of the $500K, $100K goes to marketing, trust-building and adoption. The rest funds personnel of $157.5K for 2 staff, operations of $72K for document fees, bus passes and purchased after-hours partner coverage, technology of $36K for the dashboard, and indirect costs of $54.83K at the federal de minimis rate. The remaining $79.67K is held as contingency, released only by the city contract officer. Year-1 cost per person is $3,503.
- Q: Prioritization model
  A: The page ranks options with a published points table computed in Python; no model call ranks anything. For a bed tonight, the table first removes closed sites, wrong households, unmet site conditions, wrong ages and full sites. It then weighs built for this group (40 points), free beds (20), no referral needed (20) and low-barrier entry (20). Transition programs weigh runway before the age limit (25), weeks to start (25), retention (25) and free slots (25). Doors weigh warm handoff (40), fit (30) and languages (30), favoring fit and urgency because the data shows beds that exist on paper but turn people away at the door.
- Q: Youth handoff failure analysis
  A: Youth fail at exits tied to age rather than readiness. Homelessness among youth from foster care reaches 42% by age 21, DCF IL benefits stop at 21, and close to 4 in 10 participants lose contact within 90 days post-exit. CrossRoads reports about 35% of exits without a confirmed next placement because BRIDGES has eight units, and 42% of KanCare-extension enrollees lose coverage, mostly through notices sent to old addresses. Documents compound every step: from no documents, a Kansas state ID takes at least 31 days.
- Q: Cost-of-instability analysis
  A: Python values only outcomes the program changes: ER visits avoided through kept coverage at $750 each, SNAP benefits secured, and ETV funds drawn. Without the program, those outcomes, worth an estimated $464.54K partial over 3 years ($135.96K partial in Year 1), would not happen. Stable housing is material but not valued because the data gives no local cost per shelter night, so the figure understates the true cost. The SROI ratio Python computes is 0.28 : 1 partial.
- Q: Pilot KPI framework
  A: The pilot tracks four KPIs: - Share of navigated people exiting to a confirmed next placement; target 80%, against CrossRoads' about 35% exits without one. - Share of enrolled former foster youth keeping KanCare coverage; target 90%. - Median days from intake to a Kansas state ID; target 45. - Landlord-desk reply time; target 24 hours. Leading signals are handoffs logged in the dashboard and expedited SNAP flags raised at intake.
- Q: Renewal case
  A: Renew if, by day 90, the pilot meets three targets. Placement-at-exit reaches 80%. KanCare retention reaches 90%, against today's 42% dropout. Median days to a state ID falls to 45. Sustained operation is costed at the base-case Year-3 cost per person of $2,872, with supplemental grants assumed but not yet committed.
- Q: how the 90-day pilot works
  A: The 90-day pilot runs from July to September 2026. - July: sign handoff agreements with Second Light, CrossRoads, Open Door, 211 Kansas, H.O.T., DCF IL and NEXTenant, load the dashboard, and hire staff. - August: navigators own each case until the next door confirms intake, running the City ID, birth certificate, Social Security card and state ID track and the KanCare and SNAP checklist, while the landlord desk opens. - September: follow-up checks run, KPIs are reported, and the renewal case goes to the city.
- Q: the $100K marketing allocation
  A: The $100K marketing reserve is split across 5 lines. The largest go to a NEXTenant landlord trust desk and to youth peer ambassadors with lived foster-care experience. The rest funds a wayfinding campaign at 211 Kansas, Open Door, Second Light and Center of Hope, dashboard training for case managers and H.O.T. responders, and outreach through VA, Family Promise and school liaisons. Each line has a leading indicator, such as new landlord units listed or peer-referred youth intakes, reviewed monthly.

WHAT COULD PROVE US WRONG:
  Thesis: A single named navigator who holds warm handoffs across agencies keeps youth aging out of foster care connected and moving toward housing better than the current fragmented referral chain. Would prove it wrong: Navigated youth lose contact after exit at roughly the same rate the DCF Independent Living Program reports today. Tripwire: if "Share of navigated youth exiting a program who are still in contact with their navigator at the pilot's close" is below 60% by day 60: The program shifts outreach funds to peer ambassadors for weekly in-person check-ins and reviews the caseload design with the city contract officer.
  Judge question (Problem Understanding): Who is your user, and what breaks for them? Answer: Our core user is a youth like Maya aging out of foster care, whose DCF Independent Living benefits stop at 21 while 42% of foster youth are homeless by age 21.
